questions.question: What is CrudRepository in Spring Data and what methods does it provide?
questions.title: CrudRepository in Spring Data JPA
questions.direct_answer: **`CrudRepository<T, ID>`** is Spring Data's base interface providing the core CRUD methods: `save()`, `findById()`, `findAll()`, `count()`, `delete()`, and `existsById()`. You only declare the interface with your entity type `T` and primary-key type `ID` — Spring **generates the implementation at runtime** (a dynamic proxy backed by `SimpleJpaRepository`), so there is no DAO boilerplate. Note the return types: `findById()` returns `Optional<T>` and `findAll()` returns `Iterable<T>`, not `List<T>`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the repository abstraction and that Spring auto-generates the implementation from a plain interface — no DAO code written by hand
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing a CustomerRepositoryImpl class by hand (causing a bean conflict), confusing CrudRepository with JpaRepository, or assuming findAll returns a List
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention runtime proxy generation backed by SimpleJpaRepository, the Optional return of findById that forces null-safety, and the Iterable (not List) return of findAll

sections.title: CrudRepository: The Foundation of Spring Data
sections.content:
**`CrudRepository`** is Spring Data's base interface providing the essential **CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete)** operations for any entity. Instead of writing JDBC/DAO boilerplate per table, you declare an interface extending `CrudRepository<Entity, ID>` and Spring generates a working implementation at runtime.

That's **repository abstraction**: Spring translates calls like `save()` or `findById()` into SQL through JPA and Hibernate. You get `save()` (insert/update), `findById()` (by primary key, returns `Optional`), `findAll()` (returns `Iterable`), `delete()`, `count()`, and `existsById()`. The interface is the contract; Spring provides the execution.

It sits at the bottom of the repository hierarchy. `JpaRepository` and `PagingAndSortingRepository` extend it to add paging, sorting, and JPA-specific batch methods, so anything you learn here also applies to those richer interfaces.

sections.title: CrudRepository Methods at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|save(entity)|~Insert or update|new id → INSERT|existing id → UPDATE|one method, both jobs
blue|findById(id)|~Read by PK|returns Optional<T>|never null|forces null-safety
emerald|findAll()|~Read all|returns Iterable<T>|not a List|convert or use JpaRepository
violet|delete / deleteById|~Remove|by entity or id|deleteById throws if absent|delete needs an entity
cyan|count / existsById|~Helpers|count() = long|existsById = boolean|cheap existence checks

sections.title: Declaring and Using a CrudRepository
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Writing an `Impl` class** — `CustomerRepositoryImpl` causes bean conflicts; Spring generates the implementation for you.
- **Confusing it with JpaRepository** — `CrudRepository` has no pagination/sorting or `flush()`; for those, extend `JpaRepository`.
- **Wrong ID generic** — `CrudRepository<Customer, String>` when `@Id` is `Long` fails at runtime; the second type parameter must match the id type.
- **Expecting a `List`** — `findAll()` returns `Iterable<T>`; convert it (e.g. with a loop or stream) or use `JpaRepository` for a `List`.
- **Ignoring the `Optional`** — `findById()` returns `Optional<T>`; calling `.get()` on an empty one throws `NoSuchElementException`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`CrudRepository<T, ID>`** — `T` is the entity, `ID` is the primary-key type; you declare the interface only.
- **`save()`** inserts when the id is null, updates when the id already exists.
- **`findById()` returns `Optional<T>`** — forces null-safe handling.
- **`findAll()` returns `Iterable<T>`**, not `List`.
- **Implementation is generated at runtime** via a dynamic proxy backed by `SimpleJpaRepository`.
- **It's the base interface** — `JpaRepository` extends it to add paging, sorting, and batch methods.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: CrudRepository is Spring Data's core interface that gives you the basic database operations without writing any code. I just create an interface that extends CrudRepository and specify the entity type and the id type, and Spring does the rest. It provides save for inserting or updating, findById to fetch by primary key, findAll to read everything, delete to remove records, and helpers like count and existsById. The interesting part is what happens at startup. Spring scans my interfaces, sees they extend CrudRepository, and generates a concrete implementation in memory using a proxy. That proxy is backed by a class called SimpleJpaRepository, which holds the real Hibernate logic, and it gets registered as a bean so I can inject it anywhere. I never write a repository implementation myself. For example, if I have a Customer entity with a Long id, I write interface CustomerRepository extends CrudRepository of Customer and Long, and immediately I can call save and findById. Two details worth knowing: findById returns an Optional so I'm forced to handle the missing case safely, and findAll returns an Iterable rather than a List. If I need pagination, sorting, or batch operations, I'd upgrade to JpaRepository, which extends CrudRepository and adds more methods and a List return type.

How does Spring Data generate the repository implementation?

questions.question: What does findById return and why does it return Optional?
questions.title: findById Return Type: Optional in Spring Data
questions.direct_answer: `findById()` returns **`Optional<T>`**, not `T` or `null`. This makes absence **explicit at compile time** and prevents **NullPointerException**. You unwrap it with **`orElseThrow()`** (best for REST → 404), **`orElse(default)`**, or **`map()`**. Never call **`.get()`** unguarded — on an empty Optional it throws `NoSuchElementException`, which crashes the request just like an NPE.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Optional as a null-safety contract and can unwrap it idiomatically inside a REST flow
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling .get() directly (NoSuchElementException), or using isPresent() then get() instead of functional methods like map/orElseThrow
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show orElseThrow() mapping to an HTTP 404 via @ControllerAdvice, and note Optional should only be a return type, never an entity field or parameter

sections.title: Why findById Returns Optional
sections.content:
**`Optional<T>`** (Java 8) is a container that either holds a value or is empty — it makes **null-safety explicit**. An entity may not exist, and the old `null`-return approach caused countless **NullPointerExceptions** when callers forgot to check. By returning `Optional<T>`, Spring Data forces you to acknowledge absence: you must unwrap with `isPresent()`, `orElse()`, `orElseThrow()`, or `map()` before using the value.

Spring Data uses it for every single-result query that might find nothing: `findById`, query-by-example, and custom single-object derived methods like `findByEmail`. Collection queries like `findAll` instead return an empty collection, never `null`.

sections.title: Handling Optional at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|orElseThrow()|~Must-exist case|throws on empty|maps to HTTP 404|best for REST controllers
blue|orElse(default)|~Fallback value|returns default if empty|e.g. guest profile|safe substitution
emerald|map() / flatMap()|~Transform inside|no unwrap needed|chains safely|stays Optional
rose|.get() alone|~Anti-pattern|NoSuchElementException|defeats Optional|never do this

sections.title: Wrong — .get() Without Checking
Right — orElseThrow() Maps to 404
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`.get()` without a check** — throws `NoSuchElementException`; defeats the whole point of Optional.
- **Returning `Optional<Order>` from a controller** — unwrap in the controller; return `ResponseEntity` or the entity.
- **`isPresent()` then `get()`** — verbose and error-prone; prefer `ifPresent()`, `map()`, or `orElseThrow()`.
- **Optional as an entity field or method parameter** — it's not `Serializable` and breaks JPA mapping; use it only as a return type.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`Optional<T>`** replaces `null` to make absence explicit and prevent NPEs.
- **`orElseThrow()`** is the REST default — empty → exception → HTTP 404 via `@ControllerAdvice`.
- **`orElse(default)`** supplies a fallback; **`map()`** transforms without unwrapping.
- **Never `.get()` unguarded** — it throws `NoSuchElementException`.
- **Don't use Optional** as an entity field or parameter — return type only.
- **Collection finders** return empty collections, not `Optional` and not `null`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: findById returns an Optional of the entity instead of the entity directly or null. The reason is null-safety. If a method returns null when the row doesn't exist, callers often forget to check, and you get a NullPointerException at runtime that crashes the app. Optional forces me to handle the missing case explicitly — I can't just call methods on the result, I have to unwrap it first. The most common pattern in a REST API is orElseThrow, where I throw an exception if the entity isn't found, and my exception handler turns that into a 404 response. So I'd write repository dot findById id dot orElseThrow with a lambda that builds an EntityNotFoundException. If I have a sensible default, I use orElse and provide a fallback value. And if I just want to read one field, I use map to transform the value while it's still inside the Optional, then orElse a default. The biggest mistake freshers make is calling get directly without checking. That throws a NoSuchElementException, which is just as bad as a null pointer. So I never call get on its own — I use orElseThrow, orElse, or the functional methods like map and ifPresent, which are cleaner than checking isPresent and then calling get. One more thing: Optional is meant for return types, not for entity fields or method parameters.

questions.question: What is the difference between CrudRepository, JpaRepository, and PagingAndSortingRepository?
questions.title: CrudRepository vs JpaRepository vs PagingAndSortingRepository
questions.direct_answer: It's a three-level hierarchy: **`CrudRepository`** (basic CRUD) → **`PagingAndSortingRepository`** (adds `findAll(Pageable)` and `findAll(Sort)`) → **`JpaRepository`** (adds JPA extras: `flush()`, `saveAndFlush()`, `deleteAllInBatch()`, and `List` returns). For standard Spring Data JPA, **extend `JpaRepository`** by default — it transitively includes everything below it.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the repository hierarchy and that JpaRepository transitively includes paging/sorting plus JPA batch methods
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Picking PagingAndSortingRepository for pagination without realizing JpaRepository already includes it plus batch methods and List returns
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Recommend JpaRepository as the default and explain deleteAllInBatch() vs deleteAll() for bulk performance

sections.title: The Spring Data Repository Hierarchy
sections.content:
Spring Data JPA layers three interfaces. **`CrudRepository`** is the base — `save()`, `findById()`, `deleteById()`. **`PagingAndSortingRepository`** extends it and adds `findAll(Pageable)` (pagination) and `findAll(Sort)` (sorting). **`JpaRepository`** sits on top, extending paging/sorting and adding JPA-specific methods: `flush()`, `saveAndFlush()`, `deleteAllInBatch()`, plus `List` return types.

For most Spring Boot apps you extend **`JpaRepository`** — it includes all CRUD, all paging/sorting, and the JPA extras in one place. The smaller interfaces exist mainly so non-JPA Spring Data modules (Mongo, Redis) can reuse the same hierarchy.

sections.title: Hierarchy at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|CrudRepository|~Level 1|save, findById, delete|Iterable returns|basic CRUD only
blue|PagingAndSortingRepository|~Level 2|findAll(Pageable)|findAll(Sort)|extends CrudRepository
emerald|JpaRepository|~Level 3 (top)|flush, saveAndFlush|deleteAllInBatch, List returns|the production default
violet|Rule|~What to pick|extend JpaRepository|includes everything below|drop down only if needed

sections.title: Repository Interfaces Compared
sections.content:
| Feature | CrudRepository | PagingAndSortingRepository | JpaRepository |
|---|---|---|---|
| Basic CRUD | Yes | Inherited | Inherited |
| Pagination | No | Yes (`findAll(Pageable)`) | Inherited |
| Sorting | No | Yes (`findAll(Sort)`) | Inherited |
| Batch ops | No | No | Yes (`deleteAllInBatch`) |
| Flush control | No | No | Yes (`flush`, `saveAndFlush`) |
| `findAll` returns | `Iterable<T>` | `Iterable<T>` | `List<T>` |

JpaRepository is a transitive superset of the other two.

sections.title: Limited — CrudRepository Can't Paginate
Complete — JpaRepository Has It All
When to Use Each
sections.content: Use **`CrudRepository`** only for a truly minimal service with no paging — rare in practice. Use **`PagingAndSortingRepository`** if you want paging without the JPA extras (e.g. a non-JPA Spring Data module). For standard Spring Data JPA, always extend **`JpaRepository`**: it adds `deleteAllInBatch()` (one DELETE statement for bulk cleanup), `saveAndFlush()` (force a mid-transaction sync), and convenient `List` returns. Starting with JpaRepository avoids a later interface change when you inevitably need pagination.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **CrudRepository** — basic CRUD, `Iterable` returns.
- **PagingAndSortingRepository** — adds `findAll(Pageable)` and `findAll(Sort)`.
- **JpaRepository** — adds `flush()`, `saveAndFlush()`, `deleteAllInBatch()`, `List` returns.
- **JpaRepository includes everything** below it — extend it by default.
- **`deleteAllInBatch()`** is one SQL DELETE; `deleteAll()` loads each entity first.
- **Switching later is a refactor** — start at JpaRepository to avoid it.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: These three interfaces form a hierarchy. CrudRepository is the base — it gives you the basic operations like save, findById, findAll, and deleteById. That's enough for simple cases, but most apps need more. PagingAndSortingRepository extends CrudRepository and adds two methods: findAll with a Pageable for pagination and findAll with a Sort for sorting. Those are essential for REST APIs returning large lists. At the top, JpaRepository extends PagingAndSortingRepository and adds JPA-specific methods — flush to force Hibernate to sync changes immediately, saveAndFlush to save and flush in one call, and batch operations like deleteAllInBatch that delete rows in a single SQL statement instead of loading each entity. JpaRepository also changes findAll's return type from Iterable to List, which is easier to work with. In practice, for any Spring Data JPA project I extend JpaRepository, because it includes everything from the other two plus the extras. The hierarchy exists for flexibility across different Spring Data modules, but JpaRepository is the standard choice. One thing freshers miss is that deleteAllInBatch is far faster for bulk deletes because it doesn't load entities into memory — it just runs a delete statement. And if I start with CrudRepository and later need pagination, I'd have to change the interface anyway, so starting with JpaRepository saves that rework.

questions.question: How does Spring Data JPA generate repository implementations automatically?
questions.title: How Spring Data Generates Repository Implementations
questions.direct_answer: At startup, Spring Data scans interfaces extending `CrudRepository`/`JpaRepository`, builds a **runtime proxy** for each (backed by **`SimpleJpaRepository`**), and registers it as a **bean**. There are **no generated `.class` files** — it's pure in-memory proxying. Derived method names (e.g. `findByEmail`) are parsed into queries at startup; the proxy holds an `EntityManager` to run them.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Spring's runtime proxy mechanism rather than imagining compile-time code generation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Believing Spring generates .java/.class files at build time, or writing a full Impl class for the whole interface
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name SimpleJpaRepository as the backing class, @EnableJpaRepositories as the trigger, and the proxy self-invocation caveat for @Transactional

sections.title: Proxy-Based Repository Generation
sections.content:
Spring Data JPA creates repository implementations via **runtime proxies**. At startup, the scanning triggered by **`@EnableJpaRepositories`** (auto-configured in Spring Boot) discovers every interface extending `CrudRepository`/`JpaRepository`.

For each, Spring builds a **proxy** that delegates to **`SimpleJpaRepository`** — the concrete class holding the real Hibernate/JPA logic — and registers it as a **bean**. This happens **at runtime**, not compile time: no `.class` files are generated. Derived method names like `findByEmailAndStatus` are parsed into queries during startup, and the proxy uses an injected **`EntityManager`** to execute them.

sections.title: How a Repository Call Flows
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A["@EnableJpaRepositories
(auto-configured)"] -->|"scans interfaces"| B["OrderRepository
(your interface)"] B -->|"creates"| C["Runtime proxy bean"] C -->|"delegates to"| D["SimpleJpaRepository"] D -->|"uses"| E["EntityManager"] E -->|"JDBC + dialect"| F["Database"] ```

sections.title: What Happens at Startup
sections.content:
- **Scan** — `@EnableJpaRepositories` finds repository interfaces on the classpath
- **Parse** — derived method names are validated and turned into JPQL
- **Proxy** — a proxy is created per interface, backed by `SimpleJpaRepository`
- **Register** — the proxy becomes a singleton bean, injectable by constructor
- **Run** — a call like `save()` hits the proxy → `SimpleJpaRepository.save()` → `EntityManager`

sections.title: You Declare; Spring Implements
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Writing a full `Impl` class** — `OrderRepositoryImpl` for the whole interface causes bean conflicts; implement only custom fragments.
- **Expecting compile-time code** — no `.java`/`.class` files are generated; it's runtime proxies.
- **Self-invocation surprises** — `@Transactional` works through the same proxy, so same-class internal calls bypass it.
- **Mistyping a derived method** — `findByEmial` fails at startup; Spring validates names against entity fields, so you catch the typo immediately.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Runtime proxies** are created at startup — not compile-time code generation.
- **`SimpleJpaRepository`** is the backing implementation the proxy delegates to.
- **`@EnableJpaRepositories`** triggers scanning (auto-configured in Spring Boot).
- **Derived method names** are parsed into JPQL during startup using an `EntityManager`.
- **No `.class` files** are produced; same-class self-invocation bypasses proxy behavior.
- **Custom logic** goes in a fragment interface plus an `Impl`, not the whole repository.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Spring Data JPA generates repository implementations at runtime using proxies. When the app starts, it scans for any interface that extends CrudRepository or JpaRepository. For each one, Spring creates a proxy object in memory that implements my interface, and that proxy delegates all calls to a class called SimpleJpaRepository, which contains the real database logic using Hibernate and JPA. The proxy is then registered as a bean so I can inject it anywhere. It's important that this happens at runtime, not during compilation — Spring doesn't write any Java or class files into my target folder. The whole thing is triggered by the EnableJpaRepositories annotation, which Spring Boot auto-configures. When I call repository dot save, I'm really calling a proxy method that forwards to SimpleJpaRepository dot save, which talks to the EntityManager to run the SQL. For derived queries, Spring parses the method name at startup — so findByEmailAndStatus becomes a JPQL query — and it validates the field names against my entity, which is why a typo in the method name fails fast at startup. The common misconception is that I need to write the implementation class myself. I don't. The only time I write implementation code is for a custom method Spring can't derive, and even then I implement just that one method in a separate fragment, not the whole interface. One caveat: because transactions also go through the proxy, calling a transactional repository or service method from inside the same class bypasses the proxy.

questions.question: How does Spring Data's save() method decide to INSERT or UPDATE?
questions.title: Spring Data save() INSERT vs UPDATE Decision
questions.direct_answer: `save()` checks **`isNew()`**: if the entity is new (`@Id` is `null` for object types, or `0` for primitives) it calls **`persist()`** → INSERT; otherwise it calls **`merge()`** → UPDATE. Because `merge()` does a **SELECT first**, an update is really two queries. For manually assigned IDs, implement **`Persistable`** to override `isNew()` and skip that extra SELECT.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the new-vs-existing decision and the persist/merge mechanics behind a single save() call
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming save() always inserts, or not knowing merge() runs a SELECT before the UPDATE
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain Persistable/isNew() for manually assigned IDs, and that dirty checking can update a managed entity without calling save() at all

sections.title: How save() Chooses INSERT or UPDATE
sections.content:
`save()` does both: **INSERT** for new entities, **UPDATE** for existing ones, in one call. It decides via **`isNew()`** from the `Persistable` contract. By default an entity is new when its **`@Id` is `null`** (object types) or **`0`** (primitives).

If new → `EntityManager.persist()` → INSERT (and Hibernate fills the generated id). If not new → `EntityManager.merge()` → UPDATE — and `merge()` runs a **SELECT first** to load the row. That's why you leave the id null when creating, and why repeatedly merging detached entities costs an extra query each time.

sections.title: save() Decision at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|isNew() = true|~id is null or 0|calls persist()|INSERT|id filled after save
blue|isNew() = false|~id has a value|calls merge()|SELECT then UPDATE|two queries
emerald|Dirty checking|~managed entity|no save() needed|UPDATE at commit|cheapest path
violet|Persistable|~custom isNew()|for manual IDs|avoids merge SELECT|override the default

sections.title: Inefficient — Manual ID Forces merge()'s SELECT
Efficient — Implement Persistable to Skip the SELECT
Auto-Generated ID: INSERT then UPDATE
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming save() only inserts** — a non-null id makes it an UPDATE; reusing a detached entity with an id won't INSERT.
- **Calling save() when nothing changed** — managed entities update via dirty checking at commit; an extra `save()` is redundant.
- **Manually assigned IDs** — a non-null id forces `merge()`'s SELECT-before-INSERT; implement `Persistable` to skip it.
- **Cross-transaction edits** — modifying detached entities means `merge()` does a SELECT; prefer fetching fresh in the same transaction.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`save()` is dual-purpose** — `persist()` (INSERT) for new, `merge()` (UPDATE) for existing.
- **`isNew()` default** — `@Id` null/0 means new.
- **`merge()` runs a SELECT first** — an update is an extra round trip for existing/detached entities.
- **Dirty checking** updates managed entities at commit without calling `save()`.
- **Manual IDs** — implement `Persistable.isNew()` to avoid the merge SELECT.
- **`saveAll()`** batches many saves; prefer it over `save()` in a loop.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Spring Data's save method handles both inserts and updates in one call, and it decides which by checking whether the entity is new. The default logic looks at the id field: if it's null, or zero for a primitive, the entity is considered new, so save calls persist and does an insert. If the id has a value, the entity is treated as existing, so save calls merge and does an update. For example, creating a product with a null id leads to an insert, and afterwards Hibernate fills in the generated id. For an update, I fetch by id, change a field, and call save again; since the id is set, it's a merge and an update. An important detail is that merge always runs a select first to check whether the row exists, so it's two queries. That's also why it's often better to modify an entity inside a transaction and let Hibernate's dirty checking flush the update at commit, without calling save explicitly. A common mistake is reusing an entity across transactions and expecting an insert, but getting an update because the id is set. The trickier case is manually assigned ids, like a UUID I generate in code. Since the id is non-null, save calls merge and does that wasteful select before the insert. To avoid it, I implement the Persistable interface and override isNew to return a transient flag, so save trusts me and goes straight to an insert.

questions.question: What is the difference between deleteById and delete in Spring Data?
questions.title: deleteById vs delete in Spring Data JPA
questions.direct_answer: **`deleteById(id)`** first runs a **SELECT** to load the entity (so cascades and `@PreRemove` fire), then DELETEs — two queries. **`delete(entity)`** deletes a managed entity directly — one query. On a missing id, `deleteById()` throws **`EmptyResultDataAccessException`**; `delete(null)` throws `IllegalArgumentException`. For large bulk deletes without cascades, use `deleteAllInBatch()`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know deleteById does a hidden SELECT first (for cascades/callbacks) and the differing exceptions on missing targets
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming deleteById is cheaper because it takes only an id, missing the hidden SELECT it performs
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that the load enables cascade deletes and @PreRemove, use delete() when the entity is already loaded, and deleteAllInBatch() for bulk

sections.title: Two Paths to Deletion
sections.content:
Spring Data offers **`deleteById(ID)`** and **`delete(T entity)`**. The difference is what runs before the DELETE. `deleteById()` does a **SELECT** to load the entity, confirms it exists, then DELETEs — the load is needed so Hibernate can fire **lifecycle callbacks** (`@PreRemove`) and apply **cascade deletes** to children. `delete(entity)` assumes you already hold a managed entity and skips the SELECT, going straight to DELETE.

Both remove the row; the path affects performance and referential integrity. Internally `deleteById` is essentially `findById(id).ifPresent(this::delete)`.

sections.title: deleteById vs delete at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|deleteById(id)|~SELECT then DELETE|two queries|fires cascades + @PreRemove|safe default for REST
blue|delete(entity)|~DELETE directly|one query|entity must be managed|skip when already loaded
emerald|Missing target|~error behavior|deleteById: EmptyResultDataAccessException|delete(null): IllegalArgumentException|handle for 404s
violet|Bulk|~many rows|deleteAllInBatch()|single SQL, no cascades|fastest for cleanup

sections.title: deleteById vs delete
sections.content:
| Aspect | `deleteById(id)` | `delete(entity)` |
|---|---|---|
| Queries | SELECT + DELETE (2) | DELETE only (1) |
| Needs | Just the id | A managed entity |
| If missing | `EmptyResultDataAccessException` | `IllegalArgumentException` if null |
| Cascades / `@PreRemove` | Fires (entity loaded) | Only if already managed |
| Performance | Slower (extra SELECT) | Faster if already loaded |

Use `deleteById` when you only have the id; `delete` when you've already fetched the entity.

sections.title: Wasteful — Load Then deleteById (Double SELECT)
sections.content:
```java
var order = orderRepo.findById(id).orElseThrow(); // SELECT #1
// ... validate order ...
orderRepo.deleteById(id); // deleteById does SELECT #2, then DELETE
```

sections.title: Better — Reuse the Loaded Entity with delete()
When to Use Each
sections.content: Use **`deleteById()`** when you only have the id and want Spring to verify existence, fire `@PreRemove`, and cascade to children — the typical REST delete endpoint. Use **`delete(entity)`** when you already fetched the entity (e.g. for validation) to avoid a redundant SELECT, and for `deleteAll(entities)` over a fetched set. For deleting hundreds of rows without cascades, **`deleteAllInBatch()`** issues one DELETE statement and is far faster.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking `deleteById()` is cheaper** — it does a hidden SELECT first; if you already have the entity, prefer `delete()`.
- **Not handling `EmptyResultDataAccessException`** — deleting a missing id throws; map it to a 404 instead of a 500.
- **`delete()` on a detached/null entity** — null throws `IllegalArgumentException`; ensure the entity is managed.
- **`deleteAll()` for huge sets** — it loads each entity; use `deleteAllInBatch()` for one SQL statement.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`deleteById(id)`** = SELECT + DELETE (two queries); enables cascades and `@PreRemove`.
- **`delete(entity)`** = one DELETE if the entity is managed.
- **Exceptions differ** — `EmptyResultDataAccessException` vs `IllegalArgumentException`.
- **Reuse a loaded entity** with `delete()` to avoid a redundant SELECT.
- **`deleteAllInBatch()`** is the fast path for bulk deletes (no cascades).
- **deleteById is `findById().ifPresent(delete)`** under the hood.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The main difference is what happens before the delete statement runs. When I call deleteById with an id, Spring Data first does a select to load the entity, checks that it exists, and only then issues the delete. That load is necessary because Hibernate needs the entity in its persistence context to fire lifecycle callbacks like PreRemove and to handle cascade deletes to child entities. So deleteById is actually two queries, a select and a delete. When I call delete with an entity instead, Spring assumes I already have a managed entity, so it skips the select and goes straight to the delete — one query. The exception behavior also differs. Deleting an id that doesn't exist throws EmptyResultDataAccessException, while passing null to delete throws IllegalArgumentException. In practice I use deleteById when I only have the id and want Spring to handle cascades safely, which fits a typical REST delete endpoint. I use delete when I've already loaded the entity in the same transaction, maybe to validate it first, so I don't waste a second select. A pitfall freshers hit is assuming deleteById is faster because it takes just an id, when it's actually slower because of that hidden select. And if I'm deleting hundreds of rows and don't need cascades, I reach for deleteAllInBatch, which runs a single delete statement without loading the entities at all.
